mainTopic: Dream stories and the meanings of dream images
overview: This amud opens with the end of a punishment story. It then brings a long series of dream stories. בן דמא and a heretic bring their dreams to רבי ישמעאל, and בר קפרא brings his to רבי. Some readings comfort the dreamer, while others expose his sins; in two cases the story confirms the reading with a dead man's cloak and a beam full of coins. Next come general rules about dream images such as a well, a river, a bird, and a pot. רבי יהושע בן לוי then teaches that a dreamer should rise early and say the hopeful פסוק about the image before a troubling פסוק comes first. Side teachings explain the reed, pumpkin, ox, donkey, cat, grapes, horse, ישמעאל, camel, פינחס, and elephant. Two contradictions come up along the way. The ox one is solved by asking who is riding whom. The elephant one opens with לא קשיא, and its answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The earlier story ends with a punishment
steps.stepSummary: The text finishes a story already in progress: two tied cedar trees are released and tear a man in two.
steps.simpleTranslation: After a reference to the king’s silks, the account describes two cedar trees tied together. A man’s legs are tied to the trees; when the rope is released, the trees spring back and he falls in two pieces.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of a story that began on the previous amud. The גמרא describes the punishment and then moves on to a new set of dream stories.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first words are a fragment carried over from the earlier story. The rope holds the trees together; releasing it lets each tree return to its place.

phrases.english: the king’s silks!
phrases.notes: This is the end of a sentence begun on the previous amud.

phrases.english: They tied two cedar trees with a rope,
tied one of his legs to one cedar tree
and one of his legs to the other cedar tree,
and released the rope until his head split open.

phrases.aramaic: אֲזַל כׇּל חַד וְחַד וְקָם אַדּוּכְתֵּיהּ
phrases.english: Each one went and returned to its place,
and he split and fell in two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues and closes a story that began on the previous amud.

steps.title: Fallen cheeks point to a danger that has passed
steps.stepSummary: בן דמא reports a dream about his cheeks, and רבי ישמעאל interprets it as the death of two hostile Roman groups.
steps.simpleTranslation: בן דמא, רבי ישמעאל’s nephew, asks about a dream in which both cheeks fell off. רבי ישמעאל says two Roman groups had planned harm against him, but died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new dream-interpretation story. רבי ישמעאל gives a reassuring answer to בן דמא’s disturbing dream.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dream shows a loss, but the answer places the loss with בן דמא’s enemies. The two cheeks correspond to two groups that had planned to harm him.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאַל בֶּן דָּמָא בֶּן אֲחוֹתוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
phrases.english: Ben Dama, Rabbi Yishmael’s sister’s son, asked
Rabbi Yishmael:
I saw my two cheeks fall off.
He said: Two Roman groups
planned harm against you, and died.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל בֶּן דָּמָא בֶּן אֲחוֹתוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the punishment story and begins a series of dream interpretations.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The fallen cheeks signify two hostile Roman groups that died.

steps.title: Several frightening dreams receive favorable readings
steps.stepSummary: בר קפרא tells רבי four dreams, and רבי turns each frightening image or phrase into a favorable prediction.
steps.simpleTranslation: A fallen nose means anger has gone away. Cut-off hands mean he will not need to work with his hands; severed legs mean he will ride a horse. Words that seem to predict death in אדר and no sight of ניסן are instead read as death in honor, without coming to a trial.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presents a series of questions from בר קפרא and answers from רבי. Each answer changes the apparent bad news into something favorable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the nose, רבי uses the connection between a nose and the expression for anger. For אדר and ניסן, he hears words resembling “honor” and “trial” instead of treating the month names as a timetable.

phrases.english: Bar Kappara said to Rabbi:
I saw that my nose fell off.
He said to him: Anger
has been removed from you.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: רָאִיתִי שְׁנֵי יָדַי שֶׁנֶּחְתְּכוּ.
phrases.english: He said to him: I saw my two hands cut off.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לֹא תִּצְטָרֵךְ לְמַעֲשֵׂה יָדֶיךָ.
phrases.english: He said to him: You will not need the work of your hands.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: רָאִיתִי שְׁתֵּי רַגְלַי שֶׁנִּקְטְעוּ.
phrases.english: He said to him: I saw my two legs severed.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: עַל סוּס אַתָּה רוֹכֵב.
phrases.english: He said to him: You will ride a horse.
I saw that they told me: In Adar you will die,
and you will not see Nisan.
He said to him: You will die in honor,
and you will not come to a trial.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new series of dreams with a different dreamer and interpreter.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי gives favorable meanings to each of בר קפרא’s troubling dreams.
steps.whatToRemember: In this series, an alarming dream image is not automatically given an alarming meaning.

steps.title: Oil returned to olives points to a forbidden relationship
steps.stepSummary: Another man reports pouring oil onto olives, and רבי ישמעאל interprets it as relations with his mother.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain heretic tells רבי ישמעאל that he saw himself giving oil to olives. רבי ישמעאל answers that he had relations with his mother.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new exchange with רבי ישמעאל. This time, the interpretation is an accusation rather than reassurance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Oil comes from olives; the dream pictures it going back to its source. רבי ישמעאל reads that return as pointing to the man’s mother.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל:
phrases.english: A certain heretic said to Rabbi Yishmael:
I saw myself giving oil to olives.
He said to him: You had relations with your mother.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a longer exchange with a new dreamer.

steps.title: The star dreams point to theft and sale
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל reads two star dreams as successive acts against an Israelite: stealing him, then selling him and using the proceeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: The man says he plucked a star; רבי ישמעאל says he stole an Israelite. He then says he swallowed a star; רבי ישמעאל says he sold the Israelite and consumed the money.
steps.whatsHappening: The same man brings two more dreams. רבי ישמעאל treats the second answer as continuing the act named in the first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first answer identifies the person represented by the star. The second adds what the man did afterward: he sold that person and used the payment.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: חֲזַאי דִּקְטִיף לִי כּוֹכְבָא.
phrases.english: He said to him: I saw myself plucking a star.
He said to him: You stole an Israelite.
He said to him: I saw myself swallowing the star.
He said to him: You sold the Israelite
and consumed the proceeds from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: חֲזַאי דִּקְטִיף לִי כּוֹכְבָא.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same man’s exchange with רבי ישמעאל.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The star represents an Israelite whom the man stole, then sold.

steps.title: The eyes and moon point to two relationships
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל interprets two more dreams as accusations involving the man’s sister and an Israelite woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: The man sees his eyes kissing each other; רבי ישמעאל says he had relations with his sister. He sees himself kissing the moon; רבי ישמעאל says he had relations with an Israelite woman.
steps.whatsHappening: The man continues reporting dreams, and רבי ישמעאל continues interpreting them. Both answers now concern sexual relationships.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first dream, two closely paired eyes point to siblings. In the second, רבי ישמעאל takes the moon to represent an Israelite woman.

phrases.english: He said to him: I saw my eyes
kissing one another.
He said to him: You had relations with your sister.
He said to him: I saw myself kissing the moon.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בָּא עַל אֵשֶׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל.
phrases.english: He said to him: You had relations with an Israelite woman.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: חֲזַאי עֵינַי דְּנָשְׁקָן אַהֲדָדֵי.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same series, with new dream images and new accusations.

steps.title: The myrtle shade receives a further explanation
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל first links myrtle shade to a betrothed young woman, then explains the dreamer’s added detail about the shade and tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: The man dreams that he walks in the shade of a myrtle bundle. רבי ישמעאל says he had relations with a betrothed young woman. When the man adds that the shade was above him but the bundle below him, רבי ישמעאל says his bed was upside down.
steps.whatsHappening: The dreamer gives an image, receives an answer, and then adds a detail. רבי ישמעאל uses that new detail to make the interpretation more specific.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first answer identifies the relationship at issue. The second does not replace it; it explains an additional feature of the same encounter.

keyTerms.meaning: in the shade of a myrtle bundle

phrases.english: He said to him: I saw myself walking
in the shade of a myrtle bundle.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בָּא עַל נַעֲרָה הַמְאוֹרָסָה.
phrases.english: He said to him: You had relations with a betrothed young woman.
He said to him: I saw the shade above me
while it was below me.
He said to him: Your bed was upside down.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: חֲזַאי דְּדָרֵיכְנָא בְּטוּנָא דְּאָסָא.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same exchange; the added detail sharpens the preceding interpretation.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The myrtle dream points to relations with a betrothed young woman, and its unusual arrangement adds a detail about the encounter.

steps.title: Birds around the bed point to different people’s actions
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל distinguishes ravens from doves: the first dream concerns the man’s wife, while the second concerns the man himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Ravens circling his bed mean his wife committed adultery with many men. Doves circling his bed mean he defiled many women.
steps.whatsHappening: The man reports two similar dreams about birds and his bed. רבי ישמעאל gives them different answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bed appears in both dreams, but the birds change. In the first answer, רבי ישמעאל speaks about the wife’s actions; in the second, he speaks about the dreamer’s actions.

phrases.english: He said to him: I saw ravens
circling his bed.
He said to him: Your wife committed adultery
with many men.
He said to him: I saw doves
circling his bed.
He said to him: You defiled many women.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: חֲזַאי עוֹרְבֵי דְּהָדְרִי לְפוּרְיֵיהּ.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same exchange with two closely matched dream reports.

steps.title: Two flying doves point to two wives sent away
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל interprets two doves flying from the man’s grasp as two wives he dismissed without a גט.
steps.simpleTranslation: The man sees himself holding two doves, which fly away. רבי ישמעאל says he married two women and sent them away without a divorce document.
steps.whatsHappening: The man gives one more dove dream. רבי ישמעאל now connects the two birds to two wives and their departure to being sent away without a גט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the previous dream, these doves are in the man’s hands and then leave them. The answer uses both details: there are two women, and he let them go without a גט.

phrases.english: He said to him: I saw myself holding
two doves, and they flew away.
He said to him: You married two women
and dismissed them without a divorce document.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: חֲזַאי דְּנָקֵיטְנָא תְּרֵי יוֹנֵי וּפָרְחָן.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the dove imagery, but changes the action from circling the bed to flying out of the man’s hands.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He married two women and dismissed them without a גט.
steps.whatToRemember: Small changes in a dream’s details matter here: circling doves and departing doves receive different interpretations.

steps.title: Peeling eggs points to stripping the dead
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל interprets the man's dream of peeling eggs as an act involving dead people.
steps.simpleTranslation: The man says he dreamed that he was peeling eggs. רבי ישמעאל tells him that he has stripped dead people.
steps.whatsHappening: The man reports another dream, and רבי ישמעאל gives its interpretation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The interpretation moves from an ordinary image—peeling eggs—to an accusation about the man's conduct. The next lines will show whether the man accepts it.

phrases.english: He said to him: I saw that I was peeling eggs.
He said to him: You are stripping dead people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The same series of the man's dreams and רבי ישמעאל's interpretations continues.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי ישמעאל interprets peeling eggs as stripping dead people.

steps.title: A woman confirms the disputed interpretation
steps.stepSummary: The man denies this one interpretation, but a woman identifies his cloak as belonging to a dead man he stripped.
steps.simpleTranslation: The man says that all the interpretations fit him except this one. Just then, a woman arrives and says that the cloak he is wearing belonged to a man who died and whom he stripped.
steps.whatsHappening: The man disputes the last interpretation. A woman's statement then supplies direct evidence for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dispute is about the egg dream in step 10, not the earlier dreams. The woman's identification of the cloak answers the man's denial within the story.

phrases.english: He said to him: All of them apply to me,
except for this one, which does not.
Meanwhile, this woman came
and said to him: This cloak that you are wearing—
it belongs to a certain man who died and whom you stripped.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The story tests the interpretation just given.
steps.raayaObject: The interpretation that the man stripped a dead person.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A woman identifies the cloak he is wearing as the dead man's cloak.

steps.title: A dream names a place with no known connection
steps.stepSummary: The man reports a dream about property in קפודקיא, and רבי ישמעאל checks whether the place has an ordinary connection to the family.
steps.simpleTranslation: The man says he was told in a dream that his father left him property in קפודקיא. Asked whether he has property there or whether his father went there, he answers no to both.
steps.whatsHappening: This sets up a new interpretation: רבי ישמעאל first checks whether קפודקיא can be understood as an actual place in the man's family history.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two negative answers remove the most straightforward reading of the dream. They prepare רבי ישמעאל's different reading of the place-name in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Cappadocia, the place named in the dream

phrases.english: He said to him: I saw that they were saying to me:
Your father left you property in Cappadocia.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִית לָךְ נִכְסֵי בְּקַפּוֹדְקְיָא?
phrases.english: He said to him: Do you have property in Cappadocia?
He said to him: No.
Did your father go to Cappadocia?
He said to him: No.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִית לָךְ נִכְסֵי בְּקַפּוֹדְקְיָא?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the cloak incident, the man brings another dream for interpretation.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the man or his father has a real-world connection to property in קפודקיא.

steps.title: The place-name leads to the tenth beam
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל reads the dream's place-name as a clue to a beam and the number ten; the man finds coins there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל says that קַפָּא means a beam and דֵּיקָא means ten. He tells the man to inspect the tenth beam for coins, and the man finds it full of coins.
steps.whatsHappening: Because the place itself did not fit, רבי ישמעאל interprets the sounds of its name as directions to hidden property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dream's promise of property remains relevant, but its stated location is read as a clue rather than a destination. Finding the coins confirms this reading in the story.

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן: קַפָּא כְּשׁוּרָא, דֵּיקָא עַשְׂרָה.
phrases.english: If so: Kappa means a beam; deka means ten.
Go look at the beam that is tenth,
for it is full of coins.
He went and found that it was full of coins.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן: קַפָּא כְּשׁוּרָא, דֵּיקָא עַשְׂרָה.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The negative answers make room for a reading of the dream's wording instead of its apparent geography.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The name points to the tenth beam, where the man finds the property.

steps.title: A well in a dream points to peace
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא gives a general dream interpretation and cites a verse about a well.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא says that someone who sees a well in a dream sees peace. He cites the verse in which יצחק's servants find a well of living water.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from one man's dreams to a general rule about seeing a well in a dream.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא supports the interpretation with the story of יצחק's servants finding a well. The quoted words describe the well; the association with peace comes from the wider story.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: הָרוֹאֶה בְּאֵר בַּחֲלוֹם —
phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina said: One who sees a well in a dream—
sees peace, as it is said:
“And Isaac's servants dug in the valley
and found there a well of living water.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: הָרוֹאֶה בְּאֵר בַּחֲלוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The individual dream story ends, and a collection of general dream interpretations begins.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seeing a well in a dream is interpreted as a sign of peace.

steps.title: Two more readings of the well
steps.stepSummary: רבי נתן connects the well to תורה through the word 'life'; רבא reads it as life itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי נתן says the dream means finding תורה: one verse links finding it to life, and the well verse speaks of living water. רבא says the well points to actual life.
steps.whatsHappening: Two more sages give readings of the well dream, continuing from רבי חנינא's reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי נתן links the two verses through their shared word for life, using that link to read the well as תורה. רבא instead takes the life in the well verse as actual life.

phrases.english: Rabbi Natan says: He has found Torah—
as it is said: “For one who finds me finds life,”
and it is written here: “a well of living water.”
Rava said: Actual life.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Both readings return to the well introduced in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The well may indicate finding תורה, according to רבי נתן, or actual life, according to רבא.

steps.title: Three dream images associated with peace
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנן lists a river, a bird, and a pot, then supplies a verse for each association.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנן says there are three signs of peace: a river, a bird, and a pot. He cites a verse connecting a river to peace, one describing protective birds, and one using wording associated with placing a pot and establishing peace.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new list of dream images associated with peace and shows the verse used for each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The river verse mentions peace directly. The bird verse speaks of protection; the pot connection rests on the wording תִּשְׁפֹּת in the verse.

keyTerms.meaning: You will establish; wording also associated with setting a pot in place

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חָנָן שָׁלֹשׁ שְׁלוֹמוֹת הֵן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanan said: There are three signs of peace:
a river, a bird, and a pot.
A river—as it is written:
“Behold, I extend peace to her like a river.”
A bird—as it is written:

phrases.aramaic: ״כְּצִפֳּרִים עָפוֹת כֵּן יָגֵן ה׳ צְבָאוֹת וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: “Like flying birds, so will the Lord of Hosts protect, etc.”
A pot—as it is written:
“Lord, You will establish peace for us.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָנָן שָׁלֹשׁ שְׁלוֹמוֹת הֵן:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The discussion moves from meanings of a well to a new list of peaceful dream images.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A river, bird, and pot are presented as three dream signs of peace.

steps.title: The peaceful pot must have no meat
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא limits the pot interpretation to a pot without meat and cites a troubling verse about meat in a pot.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא says the teaching about a pot applies to one without meat. He cites a verse describing people as though spread out in a pot, like meat in a cauldron.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא narrows the pot example from the previous list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pot without meat can remain a sign of peace. The cited verse gives a disturbing image of meat in a pot, so the teaching does not apply the peaceful reading to that image.

keyTerms.meaning: that has no meat in it

steps.whatToRemember: For the pot in this list, רבי חנינא specifies an empty pot, not one containing meat.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina said:
And we taught this about a pot that has no meat in it.
“And they spread them out as in a pot,
and like meat inside a cauldron.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: וּבִקְדֵרָה שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ בָּשָׂר שָׁנִינוּ.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This qualifies only the pot in the three-item list, not the river or bird.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The peaceful interpretation of a pot applies to a pot without meat.

steps.title: A river: say the verse about peace
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי gives a practical next step for someone who dreams of a river.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who sees a river in a dream should rise early and say the verse comparing peace to a river, before a troubling river verse comes to mind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from explaining dream images to telling the dreamer what to say. רבי יהושע בן לוי starts with a river.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same image appears in two verses with different meanings. The dreamer is told to say the hopeful verse first rather than leave the image open to the troubling one.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
One who sees a river in a dream should rise early and say:
“I am extending peace to her like a river,”
before another verse precedes it—
“For an adversary will come like a river.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: הָרוֹאֶה נָהָר בַּחֲלוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the earlier interpretations of dream images, this begins instructions for responding to them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After dreaming of a river, rise early and say the hopeful river verse before the troubling one.

steps.title: A bird: say the verse about protection
steps.stepSummary: The same instruction is applied to a bird in a dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who sees a bird in a dream should rise early and say the verse about hovering birds and protection, before the verse about a bird wandering from its nest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second example using the same pattern, now for a bird.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One verse connects birds with protection; the other connects a bird with being displaced. The instruction is to say the protective verse first.

phrases.english: One who sees a bird in a dream

phrases.aramaic: יַשְׁכִּים וְיֹאמַר ״כְּצִפֳּרִים עָפוֹת כֵּן יָגֵן וְגוֹ׳״,
phrases.english: should rise early and say, “Like birds flying, so will He protect, etc.”
before another verse precedes it—
“Like a bird wandering from its nest, etc.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the river example's pattern with a new dream image.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After dreaming of a bird, say the verse about protection before the verse about wandering.

steps.title: A pot: say the verse about peace
steps.stepSummary: The instruction is applied to a pot, using two verses with related wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who sees a pot in a dream should rise early and say, “Lord, You will establish peace for us,” before the verse saying, “Set on the pot, set it on.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא completes the set of river, bird, and pot from the preceding discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The hopeful verse speaks of establishing peace; the other calls for setting on a pot in a troubling passage. The earlier qualification about a pot without meat still matters when interpreting the dream.

phrases.english: One who sees a pot in a dream
should rise early and say: “Lord, You will establish peace for us,”
before another verse precedes it—
“Set on the pot, set it on.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same instruction and returns to the pot discussed just before this list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After dreaming of a pot, say the verse about establishing peace before the troubling pot verse.

steps.title: Grapes: say the verse about finding Israel
steps.stepSummary: The list extends to grapes, which also appear in a hopeful and a troubling verse.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who sees grapes in a dream should rise early and say, “Like grapes in the wilderness,” before the verse calling them grapes of poison.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds grapes to the same list of dream images.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first verse, grapes describe finding Israel with delight. In the second, the grapes are harmful; the dreamer says the first verse before that association takes hold.

phrases.english: One who sees grapes in a dream
should rise early and say, “Like grapes in the wilderness,”
before another verse precedes it—
“Their grapes are grapes of poison.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the established verse-pair pattern beyond the three images previously discussed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After dreaming of grapes, say the hopeful grape verse before the verse about poisonous grapes.

steps.title: A mountain: say the verse about good news
steps.stepSummary: A mountain can appear with good news or with mourning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who sees a mountain in a dream should rise early and say the verse about a messenger bringing good news over the mountains, before the verse about weeping over the mountains.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another verse pair, this time for a mountain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first verse places a bearer of good news on the mountains. The second speaks of weeping over them, so the dreamer is told to say the first one.

phrases.english: One who sees a mountain in a dream
should rise early and say—
“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of a bearer of good news,”
before another verse precedes it—
“Over the mountains I will raise weeping and lamentation.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another image governed by the same instruction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After dreaming of a mountain, say the good-news verse before the mourning verse.

steps.title: A shofar: say the verse about gathering
steps.stepSummary: The list contrasts a great שׁוֹפָר with a troubling call to sound one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who sees a שׁוֹפָר in a dream should rise early and say the verse about a great שׁוֹפָר being sounded, before the verse commanding a שׁוֹפָר to be sounded in גבעה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the same instruction to a שׁוֹפָר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The great שׁוֹפָר belongs to a hopeful verse about gathering the dispersed. The other sounding is part of an alarm, so the first verse is chosen.

phrases.english: One who sees a horn in a dream

phrases.aramaic: יַשְׁכִּים וְיֹאמַר ״וְהָיָה בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא יִתָּקַע בְּשׁוֹפָר גָּדוֹל״,
phrases.english: should rise early and say, “On that day a great horn will be sounded,”
before another verse precedes it—
“Sound a horn in Givah.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list with a different object but the same two-verse structure.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After dreaming of a שׁוֹפָר, say the hopeful great-שׁוֹפָר verse before the alarm verse.

steps.title: A dog: say the verse about Israel's safety
steps.stepSummary: The list pairs a quiet dog with a verse describing fierce dogs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who sees a dog in a dream should rise early and say the verse in which no dog threatens the children of Israel, before the verse about fierce dogs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the same instruction for a dog.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first verse, the dog does not even move its tongue against Israel. The second describes dogs negatively; saying the first verse supplies the hopeful association.

keyTerms.meaning: will move sharply; here, of a dog's tongue

phrases.english: One who sees a dog in a dream

phrases.aramaic: יַשְׁכִּים וְיֹאמַר ״וּלְכֹל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יֶחֱרַץ כֶּלֶב לְשֹׁנוֹ״,
phrases.english: should rise early and say, “Against any of the children of Israel, no dog will move its tongue,”
before another verse precedes it—
“And the dogs are fierce and greedy.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same pattern, now using verses that mention dogs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After dreaming of a dog, say the verse about Israel's safety before the verse about fierce dogs.

steps.title: A lion: say the verse about its roar
steps.stepSummary: This example pairs a lion's roar with a lion emerging as a threat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who sees a lion in a dream should rise early and say, “A lion has roared; who will not fear?” before the verse, “A lion has come up from its thicket.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a lion as the next dream image and gives the same instruction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chosen verse uses the lion's roar in a passage about hearing God's message. The other verse describes a lion coming out as a danger, so the dreamer says the first verse.

phrases.english: One who sees a lion in a dream

phrases.aramaic: יַשְׁכִּים וְיֹאמַר ״אַרְיֵה שָׁאָג מִי לֹא יִירָא״,
phrases.english: should rise early and say, “A lion has roared; who will not fear?”
before another verse precedes it—
“A lion has come up from its thicket.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds one more example without changing the instruction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After dreaming of a lion, say the verse about its roar before the verse about the threatening lion.

steps.title: A shave in a dream: יוסף's verse versus שמשון's verse
steps.stepSummary: Someone who dreams of a shave should say the verse about יוסף rising to greatness before the verse about שמשון losing his strength can take effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees a shave in a dream should rise early and say: 'And he shaved and changed his clothes,' before a different verse comes first: 'If I am shaved, my strength will leave me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The list goes on with a new dream image: a haircut or shave. The dreamer is told which verse to say so the dream is read in the good direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Shaving appears in two very different verses. יוסף shaved when he left prison to stand before פרעה and rise to power. שמשון said that shaving would take away his strength. Saying the good verse first is meant to set the dream's meaning on the good path.

keyTerms.meaning: Before a different verse gets there first

phrases.english: One who sees a shave in a dream,
should rise early and say:
"And he shaved and changed his clothes" (Joseph leaving prison),
before a different verse comes ahead of it:
"If I am shaved, my strength will leave me."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the same list of dream images
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dream of a shave should be paired with the verse about יוסף's rise.

steps.title: A well in a dream: living waters versus flowing wickedness
steps.stepSummary: Someone who dreams of a well should say 'a well of living waters' before the verse comparing a well to flowing evil can take effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees a well in a dream should rise early and say: 'A well of living waters,' before a different verse comes first: 'As a cistern wells up its waters.'
steps.whatsHappening: The list adds a well. Again, the dreamer is given a good verse to say before a bad one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In שיר השירים a well of living water is a picture of something pure and full of life. In ירמיה, water welling up in a cistern is compared to wickedness pouring out of ירושלים. The same image can point in either direction.

keyTerms.meaning: As a cistern wells up (pours out)

phrases.english: One who sees a well in a dream,
should rise early and say: "A well of living waters,"
before a different verse comes ahead of it:
"As a cistern wells up its waters" (so the city wells up its evil).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dream of a well should be paired with 'a well of living waters.'

steps.title: A reed in a dream: the gentle משיח versus מצרים the broken staff
steps.stepSummary: Someone who dreams of a reed should say the verse about the משיח not breaking a bruised reed, before the verse mocking מצרים as a broken reed can take effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees a reed in a dream should rise early and say: 'A bruised reed he will not break,' before a different verse comes first: 'Behold, you trust in this staff of a broken reed.'
steps.whatsHappening: The list adds a reed. The dreamer should say the good verse before the insulting one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ישעיה, the gentle redeemer is described as one who will not even break a cracked reed. In מלכים, מצרים is called a broken reed that cannot be leaned on. The good verse is about kindness, and the bad verse is about false support.

phrases.english: One who sees a reed in a dream,
should rise early and say:
"A bruised reed he will not break,"
phrases.notes: ישעיה 42:3, said in praise of the משיח

phrases.english: before a different verse comes ahead of it:
"Behold, you have trusted
in the staff of this broken reed."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the list, which leads into a ברייתא about reeds
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dream of a reed should be paired with 'a bruised reed he will not break.'

steps.title: One reed means wisdom, several reeds mean understanding
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that one reed in a dream points to חכמה and several reeds point to בינה, using a wordplay on קנה (reed) and קנה (acquire).
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: One who sees a reed in a dream may expect wisdom, as it says: 'Acquire wisdom.' Reeds: he may expect understanding, as it says: 'With all your acquisitions, acquire understanding.'
steps.whatsHappening: Because a reed was just mentioned, the גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives reeds a fully positive meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word קָנֶה (reed) sounds like קְנֵה (acquire). The verse in משלי says 'acquire wisdom,' so one reed hints at חכמה. The same verse continues 'with all your acquisitions, acquire understanding,' so many reeds (קָנִים, like קִנְיָנְךָ) hint at בינה.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not the 'say the good verse first' pattern. Here the ברייתא simply says the reed itself is a good sign, based on a wordplay.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who sees a reed (kaneh) in a dream
may expect wisdom,
as it says: "Acquire (keneh) wisdom."
Several reeds: he may expect understanding,
as it says:
"And with all your acquisitions, acquire understanding."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on the reed from the previous step with its own positive reading
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A reed means חכמה and reeds mean בינה.

steps.title: רבי זירא: four similar-sounding items are all good to dream about
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא lists pumpkin, heart of palm, wax, and reed as all being good signs in a dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: Pumpkin, heart of palm, wax, and reed are all good for a dream.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא widens the reed teaching into a short list of things that are all good signs in a dream.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These four words sound alike in Aramaic (קרא, קורא, קירא, קניא). רבי זירא says that all of them are favorable to see in a dream.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
Pumpkin, heart of palm, wax, reed:
all of them are good for a dream.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא: קָרָא, קוּרָא, קִירָא, קַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the positive reed teaching and applies it to similar items
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pumpkin, heart of palm, wax, and reed are all good dream signs.

steps.title: Pumpkins are shown only to someone who truly fears Heaven
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a dream of pumpkins is given only to a person who fears Heaven with all his strength.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: Pumpkins are shown in a dream only to one who fears Heaven with all his strength.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא adds that a pumpkin dream is a special sign, given only to a very God-fearing person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on רבי זירא's pumpkin. One explanation is that דלועין is read as hinting at the phrase 'my eyes looked up on high.' That phrase describes someone who looks to Heaven with all his heart. So the pumpkin is more than a good sign; it says something about who the dreamer is.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: It was taught:
They do not show pumpkins (in a dream)
except to one who is
God-fearing with all his strength.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a special point about one item, the pumpkin, from רבי זירא's list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A pumpkin dream is shown only to a person who fully fears Heaven.
steps.whatToRemember: Reeds mean חכמה and בינה. רבי זירא says four similar plants are all good signs. Pumpkins appear only to the truly God-fearing.

steps.title: An ox in a dream: majesty versus goring
steps.stepSummary: The list returns to its pattern: someone who dreams of an ox should say 'his firstborn ox, majesty is his' before 'if an ox gores a man.'
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees an ox in a dream should rise early and say: 'His firstborn ox, majesty is his,' before a different verse comes first: 'If an ox gores a man.'
steps.whatsHappening: After the side teachings, the גמרא goes back to its main list of paired verses and adds the ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברכה of משה to יוסף, the ox stands for royal glory. In the laws of damages, an ox is the animal that gores and kills. The dreamer should say the glorious verse first.

phrases.english: One who sees an ox in a dream,
should rise early and say:
"His firstborn ox, majesty is his,"
before a different verse comes ahead of it:
"If an ox gores a man."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the paired-verse list after the side teachings about reeds and pumpkins
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dream of an ox should be paired with 'his firstborn ox, majesty is his.'

steps.title: Five ways an ox can appear in a dream and what each means
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists five ox dreams. Eating its meat means wealth. Being gored means sons who debate תורה. Being bitten means suffering. Being kicked means a long journey. Riding it means rising to greatness.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: Five things were said about an ox. One who eats from its meat will become rich. If it gored him, he will have sons who 'gore' each other in תורה. If it bit him, suffering will come to him. If it kicked him, a long journey awaits him. If he rode it, he will rise to greatness.
steps.whatsHappening: Just as with the reed, the ox from the list leads into a ברייתא. This one explains what different ox dreams mean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The meaning depends on what the ox does in the dream, not just on seeing it. Even goring, which sounds bad, is turned into something good: sons who argue sharply in learning. Biting and kicking stay as warnings, while eating and riding are signs of success.

keyTerms.meaning: Who 'gore', that is, debate sharply, in תורה

steps.confusionAlert: Being gored by an ox in a dream is a good sign here (sons strong in תורה), even though the verse 'if an ox gores a man' in the previous step was the bad one.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Five things were said about an ox (in a dream).
One who eats from its meat will become rich.
If it gored him, he will have sons
who 'gore' each other in Torah debate.
If it bit him, suffering is coming upon him.
If it kicked him, a long journey awaits him.
If he rode it, he will rise to greatness.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: חֲמִשָּׁה דְּבָרִים נֶאֶמְרוּ בְּשׁוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on the ox from the previous step with a detailed list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox dream's meaning depends on the action: eating means wealth, goring means Torah-learning sons, biting means suffering, kicking means a long journey, and riding means greatness.
steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא's pattern: an image is listed with a good and a bad verse, and then a ברייתא sometimes gives it its own detailed positive reading (reed, then ox).

steps.title: Another source says riding an ox means death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the previous ברייתא with another ברייתא that says riding an ox in a dream means death.
steps.simpleTranslation: But wasn't it taught in a ברייתא: if he rode it, he will die!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a contradiction. Step 33 said riding an ox means rising to greatness, but another ברייתא says it means death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same dream picture, riding an ox, seems to get two opposite meanings. One source says it is very good and the other says it is very bad. The גמרא needs to explain how both can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: But wasn't it taught (in a ברייתא)? This phrase introduces a contradicting source.

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught: if he rode it, he will die!
phrases.notes: This contradicts 'rode it, he will rise to greatness' from Step 33.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the last item of the ox list in Step 33.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that riding an ox in a dream means rising to greatness.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two ברייתות give opposite meanings to the same dream.

steps.title: It depends on who is riding whom
steps.stepSummary: If he rides the ox, it means greatness. If the ox rides him, it means death.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is when he rides the ox. That one is when the ox rides him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction by saying the two sources describe two different dreams.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two sources are not about the same picture. When the person is on top, controlling the ox, it is greatness. When the ox is on top of him, it is death. The contradiction disappears.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. This phrase introduces an answer that splits the cases.

phrases.english: It is not difficult,
this is where he rides the ox,
that is where the ox rides him.

steps.whatToRemember: Riding an ox means greatness. Being ridden by an ox means death.
steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא דְּרָכֵיב הוּא לְתוֹרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (two different dream scenarios)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to describe the same dream of riding an ox.
steps.terutzMaskana: The person riding the ox is a good sign. The ox riding the person is a sign of death.

steps.title: Donkey: expect salvation
steps.stepSummary: Seeing a donkey in a dream means one should expect salvation, based on the פסוק about the משיח riding a donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees a donkey in a dream should expect salvation, as it says: 'Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and saved is he, poor and riding on a donkey.'
steps.whatsHappening: The list of dream signs continues. A donkey points to salvation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof comes from a פסוק in זכריה about the king, the משיח, coming on a donkey and bringing salvation. Because the donkey appears together with salvation in the פסוק, it becomes a sign of salvation.

phrases.english: One who sees a donkey in a dream —
should expect salvation,
as it is said: 'Behold, your king comes to you,'
righteous and saved is he,
poor and riding upon a donkey.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ox discussion is resolved, the list moves on to a new animal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A donkey in a dream is a sign of salvation.

steps.title: Cat: it depends on the local word for cat
steps.stepSummary: Where a cat is called שונרא, the dream means a nice song. Where it is called שינרא, the dream means a bad change.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees a cat in a dream: in a place where they call it 'שונרא,' a nice song (שירה נאה) will be made for him. Where it is 'שינרא,' he will have a bad change (שינוי רע).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the meaning of a cat dream. The meaning depends on what the cat is called in the dreamer's local language.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is wordplay. 'שונרא' sounds like 'שירה נאה,' a nice song. 'שינרא' sounds like 'שינוי רע,' a bad change. So the same animal can be a good or bad sign depending on the local word for it.

keyTerms.meaning: Two local Aramaic words for a cat
A nice song (a pleasant song of praise)

phrases.english: One who sees a cat in a dream —
in a place where they call it 'shunra' —
a nice song will be made for him.
Where it is 'shinra' — he will undergo a bad change.

steps.confusionAlert: The animal itself is the same in both cases. Only the local word for it changes, and that is what flips the meaning.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of dream signs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The meaning of a cat dream follows the sound of the local word for cat.

steps.title: Grapes: color and season matter
steps.stepSummary: White grapes are always good. Black grapes are good in their season and bad out of season.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees grapes in a dream: white ones, whether in season or not, are good. Black ones in season are good. Out of season, they are bad.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains grape dreams using two details: the color of the grapes and whether they are in season.
steps.deeperAnalysis: White grapes are a good sign no matter when they appear. Black grapes are good only in their season. Seeing them out of season is a bad sign.

phrases.english: One who sees grapes in a dream, white ones,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין בִּזְמַנָּן, וּבֵין שֶׁלֹּא בִּזְמַנָּן — יָפוֹת.
phrases.english: whether in their season or not in their season — they are good.
Black ones in their season — good.
Not in their season — bad.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of dream signs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: White grapes are always good. Black grapes are good only in their season.

steps.title: Horse: color and speed matter
steps.stepSummary: A white horse is good whether walking or running. A red horse is good walking but bad running.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees a white horse in a dream, whether walking calmly or running, it is good for him. A red one walking is good. Running is bad.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains horse dreams using the horse's color and how fast it is moving.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same pattern as the grapes. One version, the white horse, is always good. The other version, the red horse, depends on a second detail. A red horse running fast is a bad sign.

phrases.english: One who sees a white horse in a dream,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין בְּנַחַת, בֵּין בְּרָדוּף — יָפֶה לוֹ.
phrases.english: whether walking calmly or running — it is good for him.
A red one, walking calmly — good,
running — harsh.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of dream signs, with the same pattern as the grapes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A white horse is always good. A red horse is good only when walking calmly.

steps.title: ישמעאל: prayer will be heard, but only the real ישמעאל
steps.stepSummary: Seeing ישמעאל means one's prayer is heard. This applies only to ישמעאל the son of אברהם, not to just any Arab.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees ישמעאל in a dream, his prayer is heard. This is specifically ישמעאל the son of אברהם, but a regular Arab does not count.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the meaning of seeing ישמעאל in a dream, and then right away limits it to the actual ישמעאל from the Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name ישמעאל means 'God hears,' so it points to a prayer being heard. The גמרא then narrows the rule: it only counts if the dreamer sees the ישמעאל of the Torah, the son of אברהם, and not a random Arab.

keyTerms.meaning: ישמעאל, son of אברהם (the name means 'God hears')

phrases.english: One who sees Ishmael in a dream —
his prayer is heard.
phrases.notes: This is based on the name, which means 'God hears.'

phrases.english: And specifically Ishmael son of Abraham,
but just any Arab — no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of dream signs and adds a limit to this one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seeing the real ישמעאל, son of אברהם, means one's prayer is heard. Seeing an ordinary Arab does not carry this sign.

steps.title: Camel: death was decreed but he was saved
steps.stepSummary: Seeing a camel means death had been decreed on the dreamer, but he was rescued from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees a camel in a dream, death was decreed on him from Heaven, and they saved him from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the meaning of a camel dream. The next two steps will each bring a פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sign has two parts: a decree of death, and a rescue from that decree. The two אמוראים that follow each look for a פסוק that hints at this through the word גמל, camel.

phrases.english: One who sees a camel in a dream —
death was decreed upon him from Heaven
and they saved him from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of dream signs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A camel in a dream means a decree of death was cancelled.

steps.title: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא: the source is 'גם עלה'
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא finds the camel hint in the words גם עלה, 'also bring up,' from ה׳'s promise to יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא said: What is the פסוק? 'I will go down with you to מצרים, and I will also surely bring you up (גם עלה).'
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא brings a פסוק as the source for the camel sign.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'גם עלה' sound like 'גמל,' camel. In the פסוק, ה׳ promises יעקב that he will go down and also be brought back up. That matches the idea of falling into danger and then being lifted out of it.

keyTerms.meaning: Also surely bring up. It sounds like גמל.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥama son of Rabbi Ḥanina said:
What is the verse?
'I will go down with you into Egypt,'
'and I will also surely bring you up.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: מַאי קְרָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a pasuk source for the camel sign in Step 41.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The camel sign is hinted at in the words גם עלה.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק: the source is 'גם... לא תמות'
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק brings a different פסוק, where ה׳ 'also' (גם) removes דוד's sin and he will not die.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: The source is from here: 'ה׳ has also (גם) removed your sin; you will not die.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives a different פסוק as the source for the camel sign.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק was said to דוד: he deserved death, but he was spared. That fits the 'death decreed, then saved' meaning even more directly. The hint word here is just גם, which is part of גמל.

keyTerms.meaning: From here (this introduces a different source)

phrases.aramaic: רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק אָמַר: מֵהָכָא:
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: From here:
'The Lord also has put away your sin;'
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 12:13. It was said to דוד.

phrases.english: 'you shall not die.'

steps.whatToRemember: A camel (גמל) means a death decree was cancelled. It is hinted at in גם עלה or in גם... לא תמות.
steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק אָמַר: מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different pasuk from the one in Step 42.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The camel sign comes from the פסוק where ה׳ spares דוד from death.

steps.title: פינחס: a miracle will happen
steps.stepSummary: Seeing פינחס in a dream means a miracle will be done for the dreamer.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees פינחס in a dream, a miracle will be done for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The list continues with a person from the Torah. פינחס points to a miracle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Miracles happened for פינחס when he acted with zeal. So seeing him is a sign that a miracle will be done for the dreamer, just as miracles were done for him.

phrases.english: One who sees Pinehas in a dream —
a miracle is performed for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of dream signs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פינחס in a dream is a sign of a miracle.

steps.title: Elephant: miracles, and more elephants mean more miracles
steps.stepSummary: One elephant (פיל) means miracles. Many elephants mean miracles upon miracles.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees an elephant in a dream, miracles are done for him. Elephants: wonders upon wonders are done for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the meaning of elephant dreams, again using wordplay with פלא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פיל, elephant, sounds like פלא, miracle. One elephant means miracles. Several elephants mean even more: miracles on top of miracles.

phrases.english: One who sees an elephant in a dream —
miracles are performed for him.
Elephants — wonders upon wonders are performed for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the miracle theme from פינחס in Step 44.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An elephant means miracles. Many elephants mean wonders upon wonders.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the elephant is not a good dream sign
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges Step 45 with a ברייתא saying all animals are good in a dream except the elephant and the monkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: But wasn't it taught in a ברייתא: All kinds of animals are a good sign in a dream, except for the elephant and the monkey!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks what it just said, that an elephant in a dream means miracles. It quotes a ברייתא that singles out the elephant as one of only two animals that are NOT good to dream about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 45 said a פיל is a very good sign: miracles, or even miracles upon miracles. The ברייתא says almost every animal is a good sign, but the פיל and the קוף are the exceptions. That makes the elephant look bad, which directly contradicts Step 45.

keyTerms.meaning: But wasn't it taught in a ברייתא? (opening of a challenge from a source)
good (a good sign) for a dream

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא does not say all animals are bad. It says the opposite: all animals are GOOD, and only the elephant and monkey are the exceptions. The problem is that the elephant is one of those exceptions.

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught in a baraita:
All kinds of animals are a good sign in a dream,
except for the elephant and the monkey!
phrases.notes: The elephant is listed as an exception, so it is not a good sign. This clashes with Step 45.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the statement in Step 45 that an elephant in a dream means miracles.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 45: seeing an elephant in a dream means miracles.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא lists the elephant as an exception to the rule that animals are good dream signs. That implies an elephant is not a good sign, which contradicts Step 45.

steps.title: The גמרא says the contradiction is not a problem
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens its answer with 'לא קשיא', signaling that both sources can be reconciled. The details follow on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא announces that the contradiction can be solved, and the explanation of how comes right on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לא קשיא' tells us the גמרא will not reject either source. It will usually explain that each source is talking about a different case. Here that would mean a different way of seeing the elephant.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not difficult; the formula that opens a resolution splitting two sources into different cases

steps.confusionAlert: Do not stop here thinking the answer is finished. 'לא קשיא' only promises an answer. The actual distinction comes next.

phrases.english: It is not difficult,
phrases.notes: The answer itself comes in the next line.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the challenge raised in Step 46.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case distinction (two different situations), to be spelled out next
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא and Step 45 seem to give opposite meanings to dreaming of an elephant.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both sources stand. They apply to different situations, which the גמרא is about to explain.
